summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
The U.S. Government Accountability Office documented that twenty of twenty-three major federal agencies reported approximately 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, while three agencies reported having no uses for AI at all. Of those reported cases, only about 200 were in active production, meaning most remained in planning phases at the time of the audit. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of use cases, with applications spanning analysis of drone photography, processing of large datasets, identification of border activities through cameras and radar, and targeting of scientific specimens for planetary rovers. The GAO also found meaningful gaps in how agencies track their own activity, with only five of twenty agencies providing comprehensive and accurate inventory data, and two agencies including systems that were later determined not to be AI at all.

Federal compliance with existing AI requirements has been uneven. Ten of the twenty-three agencies reviewed had implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, twelve implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. The General Services Administration established an AI Center of Excellence and the Department of Commerce created a plan to develop AI technical standards, both meeting their selected requirements in full. However, the Office of Management and Budget had not yet developed government-wide guidance for the acquisition and use of AI, and the Office of Personnel Management had not established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work. The GAO noted that without consistent acquisition guidance, agencies cannot manage AI in a coordinated or effective way.

The President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included 1.8 billion dollars for nondefense research and development investment in AI, signaling federal intent to expand the technology's role even as governance frameworks remain incomplete. Operationally, agencies are using AI to identify information security threats and facilitate review of large datasets, among other functions. The GAO's broader conclusion was that while agencies have taken initial steps, safeguards needed to manage AI's risks and societal consequences are not yet fully in place, and incomplete inventories directly hinder the government's ability to manage what it has already deployed.

On the international side, Oxford Insights produces the Government AI Readiness Index, which scores nearly every country on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption and serves as the standard cross-national comparison for how prepared governments are to implement AI at scale. The OECD.AI Policy Observatory complements this by tracking national AI strategies, public-sector initiatives, and ethical frameworks across member and partner countries, and gives access to more than 900 national AI policies and initiatives. Stanford HAI's annual AI Index carries a government and policy track covering legislation counts, national strategy execution, and public-sector procurement, and the 2026 edition notes a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared institutions are to manage it.

For anyone assessing whether to deploy AI in or alongside a government context, the regulatory environment is both active and unsettled. The theworldofai.org AI Laws section tracks 2,432 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, updated daily, which reflects the pace at which state legislatures are writing new requirements even as federal guidance remains incomplete. The OECD.AI framework describes the policy goal as developing AI that is fair, transparent, explainable, robust, secure, and safe, but translating those principles into operational procurement standards is still a work in progress across most governments. The practical picture is one of genuine momentum in adoption paired with real institutional immaturity in governance, a combination that creates both opportunity and measurable compliance risk for public-sector vendors and agencies alike.
